title: Audio Range Cartographer
user: Indie game sound designers using spatial audio who need to see and tune where a sound is audible before repeatedly running through a scene.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Web Audio developer explicitly asks where people lose track of what is happening in audio graphs and what takes the most time to debug.
The proposal says spatial-audio max distance and attenuation are only numeric values today and requests editor/runtime visualisation; it has 22 reactions.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 implementation requests, one from browser audio and one from a game engine; spatial-audio mistakes are time-consuming to hear and verify in context.
current_workaround: Change numeric attenuation settings, run the scene, move the player manually, and listen; some teams draw approximate circles by hand.
incumbents_and_gap: Godot debug shapes and Web Audio Studio expose parts of the problem, but neither makes a compact, engine-neutral audio-placement review artifact from scene coordinates and attenuation curves.
smallest_useful_product: An offline web tool that imports a tiny CSV/JSON scene map, lets a designer place emitters and attenuation curves, then exports a labelled PNG/SVG audibility map and a shareable preset. Non-goals: audio playback engine, DAW, or AI sound generation.
success_measure: In a pilot, a designer produces a useful placement map in under 10 minutes and catches at least one overlapping, inaudible, or over-wide emitter before a playtest.
monetization: one-time — it is a local production utility with episodic project value and no reason to retain level data.
constraints: All maps and coordinates stay in-browser; curve semantics must be labelled rather than pretending different engines attenuate identically; import untrusted files safely.
why_distinct: It turns spatial-audio tuning into a reviewable visual artifact rather than another node editor or audio workstation.

title: Kindred Co-op
user: A parent and child playing apart who want a short, kind remote co-op game without ads, data harvesting, subscriptions, or complex controls.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent asks for remote co-op with a 10-year-old and reports finding a market full of dark patterns, data harvesting, recurring fees, and unreliable servers.
A game-developer request says large multi-action input maps are difficult to grasp and asks for a visual representation of keyboard, mouse, and controller controls.

recurrence: One direct family buyer request plus an independent game-input usability request in 2026; the severity is trust and usability rather than lack of another large game catalog.
current_workaround: Search app stores, tolerate ads or subscriptions, use a larger co-op game, or play the same single-player seed while talking.
incumbents_and_gap: The Past Within and Terraria are recommended by players, while common mobile titles optimize engagement and monetization. The gap is a small, browser-first asynchronous/real-time co-op experience with a parent-readable privacy promise and visual control onboarding.
smallest_useful_product: A two-player invite-link PWA with three 15-minute asymmetric picture-and-signal puzzles, illustrated first-run control cards, no account, and a host-controlled session expiry. Non-goals: chat network, user-generated content, loot loops, or ad SDKs.
success_measure: At least 40% of first sessions finish two puzzles, and 70% of surveyed parents say they understood data handling and controls without assistance.
monetization: one-time — a clear paid family game aligns with the explicit rejection of recurring fees and data-funded play.
constraints: Use minimal invite tokens, no behavioural analytics, no open chat, age-appropriate content, and clearly describe parental-device responsibility; WebRTC/WebSocket relay must expire sessions.
why_distinct: The product is deliberately a bounded, privacy-minimal co-op ritual, not a monetized casual-game platform.

title: PairPlay Motion
user: Friends and families with spare phones or split Joy-Cons who want a frictionless motion-controller party-game setup in a browser.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user seeks genuinely off-the-beaten-path projects for disused phones beyond the usual camera, reader, gaming-device, and photo-frame ideas.
A Godot request explains that pairing Joy-Cons blocks games from using each sensor separately for motion and local multiplayer.

recurrence: Two 2026 signals around underused mobile hardware and separable motion inputs; setup friction prevents a potentially playful device capability from being used.
current_workaround: Install a platform-specific remote-control app, pair Bluetooth controllers, or avoid motion mechanics altogether.
incumbents_and_gap: Jackbox uses phones but mostly for text prompts; Steam Link and console pairing are heavyweight. There is no small browser kit that treats two phones or split controllers as calibrated, privacy-local motion inputs for a room-scale microgame.
smallest_useful_product: A QR-pairing PWA with a host screen, two-phone motion calibration, and three original 2–4 player reaction games; it runs over local Wi-Fi and shows an explicit permission screen. Non-goals: controller driver, social network, or copyrighted console emulation.
success_measure: Two first-time players reach a calibrated playable round within 90 seconds on supported mobile browsers, with at least 80% completing a five-minute session.
monetization: one-time — a small party-game collection should be understandable and usable without a subscription.
constraints: Motion-sensor access requires browser permission and iOS-specific handling; use LAN/WebRTC where possible, do not retain sensor streams, and disclose that low-end devices vary.
why_distinct: It makes unusual input the game mechanic, rather than shipping another controller-mapping utility or clone of a party-game franchise.

title: A11y Playtest Captioner
user: Browser-game creators who need to author and hear concise, multilingual descriptions for important visual game states before inviting disabled playtesters.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solo accessibility developer built a GPU-accelerated select-to-speak overlay because they could not access PC-game text with available open-source tools.
p5.js maintainers are asked to add language metadata to visual descriptions because screen readers otherwise mispronounce or skip non-English text.

recurrence: Two 2026 accessibility requests at different layers: players need access to visual game text, and creators need descriptions that work in the right spoken language.
current_workaround: Add alt-like text ad hoc, test only with browser devtools, rely on a generic OCR overlay, or postpone accessibility until late playtesting.
incumbents_and_gap: Game Accessibility Guidelines provide advice and screen readers read DOM; neither gives canvas-game creators a lightweight state-to-description editor and keyboard review loop.
smallest_useful_product: An npm library plus local preview page: developers register named canvas/game states, write localized descriptions and focus order, then test them with keyboard navigation and browser speech synthesis. Non-goals: OCR, automatic accessibility claims, or replacing disabled playtesters.
success_measure: A pilot game adds descriptions for ten critical states in under one hour, and a keyboard-only reviewer can identify the active objective and available actions in 90% of scripted states.
monetization: free — an open integration layer needs wide adoption; paid audits can be considered separately.
constraints: Do not claim WCAG or game-accessibility compliance; descriptions must be author-controlled, localized strings need language tags, and speech synthesis stays on device.
why_distinct: It helps authors expose intentional game state, rather than attempting an unreliable AI screen reader for arbitrary games.

title: Creative Cartridge
user: Parents setting up an old computer for a 4–7-year-old who want a finite, offline creative play space rather than an internet feed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent wants an old living-room computer with downloadable offline games/content but no endless scrolling, and asks what OS or userland setup people use.
p5.js users request selectable custom builds because a 1 MB minified bundle is steep even for a small animated logo.

recurrence: A direct 2026 parenting request and a 2025 browser-creative-coding distribution concern point to a small, low-bandwidth offline bundle rather than a new child-facing feed.
current_workaround: Install a child-focused Linux distribution, bookmark websites, download scattered games, or hand over a tablet with restricted browsing.
incumbents_and_gap: Endless OS, GCompris, Scratch, and Edubuntu are broad environments. The unresolved gap is a parent-curated, one-folder creative cartridge that launches offline without a desktop-admin project or online discovery surface.
smallest_useful_product: A downloadable PWA bundle with six tiny local activities (sound painting, shape stories, camera-free stop-motion cards, rhythm pads), a parent PIN for cartridge selection, and an offline health check. Non-goals: browser filtering, accounts, ads, analytics, or an app store.
success_measure: A parent can install a cartridge on an old laptop in under 15 minutes and a child completes three activities during one offline week without opening a web browser.
monetization: one-time — content packs have clear finite value and the safety proposition is stronger without ongoing child profiling.
constraints: No collection of child data; fully usable offline after installation; large assets need a small-download mode; parent PIN is a convenience, not a security boundary.
why_distinct: It is a deliberately finite creative environment, not another educational-content platform or kids’ browser.

title: Doodle to Game
user: An adult making a first tiny game with a child who needs the child’s drawings to become playable assets without learning an engine or managing art files.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An adult asks for a stack to make a visual game with an 11-year-old in a weekend, saying Godot has too much setup and asset management is a concern.
A 41-reaction tablet-support collection identifies missing pen/finger differentiation, palm rejection, gestures, and heavy-stroke performance as drawing-tool gaps.

recurrence: A direct child game-making request and a high-interest tablet-drawing gap show that sketching is approachable while asset-to-game plumbing is not.
current_workaround: Use Scratch stickers, hunt for free assets, scan and crop drawings manually, or spend the session configuring a game engine.
incumbents_and_gap: Scratch and p5.js can make games, while Procreate/Excalidraw capture drawings. None centers the short workshop flow: draw a character, assign one behaviour, and immediately play it in a fixed template.
smallest_useful_product: A tablet-friendly offline PWA with three fixed games (dodge, collect, top-down maze). It captures a drawing or photo of paper art, removes a simple background locally, assigns it to a sprite, and exposes only speed, score, and sound controls. Non-goals: general game engine, public gallery, AI image generation, or cloud asset storage.
success_measure: A child and adult make a playable, personalized game in 45 minutes, with the child drawing at least two assets and changing one rule themselves.
monetization: one-time — a workshop tool is episodic and should not require an account for a family activity.
constraints: Process camera images locally; clearly warn that background removal is best on high-contrast paper; no uploaded child artwork; accessible touch targets and undo are required.
why_distinct: It makes a child’s physical drawing the asset pipeline, not a broad coding course or generic drawing app.

title: Multiplayer Camera Kit
user: Developers of small browser 2D co-op games who need a safe, inspectable camera that keeps several players visible without rebuilding framing math.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer asks which frameworks people use to create multiplayer 2D browser games, beyond PhaserJS.
A local-multiplayer developer calls multi-target camera scripting a massive hurdle and requests automatic bounding-box framing and zoom.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 game-development requests: choosing a browser multiplayer stack and avoiding heavy camera calculations for multi-character play.
current_workaround: Copy a camera gist, hand-code bounds and smoothing, hard-code split-screen thresholds, and tune it only after players fall off-screen.
incumbents_and_gap: Phaser, PixiJS, and Godot expose cameras but leave product-specific multi-target policies to each game. Existing snippets rarely provide a visible safety envelope or deterministic replay tests.
smallest_useful_product: An npm package for Canvas/WebGL games that takes player rectangles and world bounds, outputs camera position/zoom plus a debug overlay and deterministic trace runner. Non-goals: networking, rendering engine, split-screen renderer, or physics.
success_measure: A sample Phaser/Pixi game reaches stable two-to-four-player framing in under 30 lines of integration, and a supplied replay catches a deliberate off-screen regression.
monetization: free — engine-agnostic primitives benefit from open adoption; paid support is optional later.
constraints: Document coordinate and aspect-ratio assumptions; no player telemetry; preserve deterministic behaviour across frame rates; provide accessibility-safe zoom limits.
why_distinct: It is a narrowly scoped, testable multi-target camera policy rather than another game framework.

title: Line Take Match
user: Indie animators and game creators recording character lines who need to compare takes for level, pace, and emotional consistency without cloning anyone’s voice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An animator reports inconsistent, flat AI voice results and expensive unusable human takes across roughly 40 lines, and asks for a better workflow.
A puzzle-game developer says stream-level volume control is missing, making audio implementation and iteration tedious; the request has 18 reactions.

recurrence: Two independent production problems across 2025–26: iterating audio assets and keeping many dialogue lines usable, rather than merely generating more speech.
current_workaround: Keep naming conventions and notes, compare waveforms in a DAW, normalize manually, then discover level or pace mismatches in the edit.
incumbents_and_gap: Audacity and DAWs edit audio; ElevenLabs and other generators create voices. The gap is a consent-safe, local takeboard specifically for comparing delivery against a chosen reference line, not generating or impersonating a voice.
smallest_useful_product: A local web app that imports creator-owned WAV/MP3 takes, groups them by line, shows loudness, duration, pause, and pitch-range comparison against a selected approved take, and exports a handoff CSV. Non-goals: speech generation, voice cloning, transcription service, or cloud hosting.
success_measure: A creator labels and compares 40 lines in under 30 minutes and flags at least five materially inconsistent takes before export.
monetization: one-time — local media analysis is an editing utility, and creators should not have to upload unreleased dialogue.
constraints: Process audio locally; obtain performer consent for all material; present measurements as review cues rather than quality scores; respect licensed-music and performer-rights boundaries.
why_distinct: It improves human creative direction and take selection without being a thin generative-voice wrapper.

title: Live Figure Deck
user: Scientists and educators who need a few formula-driven, animated explanatory figures in a talk without adopting a full animation pipeline.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A scientific presenter says Beamer is cumbersome for formulas, graphs, and animation, while Manim may be too much, and asks for alternatives.
A 2026 animation request describes the difficulty of representing start/end state over a duration and the risk of corrupted animation state with point events.

recurrence: Two 2026 requests about animation that is communicative rather than decorative: a presenter needs simple animated figures and a creator needs reliable duration semantics.
current_workaround: Use Beamer/TikZ, hand-code D3 or p5, export a Manim movie, or paste a static image into slides.
incumbents_and_gap: Manim is powerful but code-heavy; Quarto is document-centric; PowerPoint is awkward for formulas. The gap is a small offline authoring surface for one interactive mathematical figure with a clean present/export mode.
smallest_useful_product: A static web editor with formula labels, a 2D plot, parameter sliders, named animation intervals, and export to a self-contained HTML slide or MP4-ready frame sequence. Non-goals: general slideware, CAS, AI lesson authoring, or hosted collaboration.
success_measure: A researcher reproduces one explanatory moving figure from a recent talk in under an hour and exports it without a runtime server.
monetization: one-time — individual educators need durable local exports, not a presentation subscription.
constraints: Math rendering must work offline; label animation intervals precisely; export must be deterministic; do not imply mathematical correctness beyond user-entered equations.
why_distinct: It sits between static charts and a full animation/code studio, optimized for one explainable figure.

title: Canvas Regression Reel
user: Solo browser-game developers who need visual evidence of rendering regressions, not just headless logic tests and a pile of manual screenshots.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solo browser-game developer says visual verification of every feature and bug makes them the bottleneck and asks how to continuously catch visual regressions.
A 186-reaction Godot proposal describes confusing play/run configurations and notes that professional developers build plugins to manage what scene runs and with which properties.

recurrence: A direct 2026 solo-developer request and a high-reaction run/debug workflow issue point to repeatable visual execution as a persistent game-tooling gap.
current_workaround: Rerun the game manually, save screenshots by hand, use headless bots for logic only, or accept visual checks late in the release cycle.
incumbents_and_gap: Playwright and Percy target DOM apps; engine test runners focus on unit/logic tests. The gap is a compact canvas-oriented replay that records specified input frames and displays the first divergent image region as a short reel.
smallest_useful_product: An npm recorder/reporter for browser canvas games: capture a seeded input trace, render checkpoint PNGs, compare tolerantly, and emit a self-contained HTML reel. Non-goals: cloud test farm, autonomous bug fixing, asset hosting, or a game engine.
success_measure: On a seeded demo, the tool identifies the first changed checkpoint and creates a reviewable report in CI under two minutes.
monetization: free — local/CI adoption is the key; hosted artifact retention could be an optional later service.
constraints: Require deterministic seed hooks where possible; mask user-supplied assets in reports; make pixel tolerance explicit; never upload build artifacts by default.
why_distinct: It is a game-frame replay and diagnosis artifact, not generic visual-regression SaaS or an AI playtester.

title: Photo Walk Scratchbook
user: Photographers trying to make deliberate pictures with a real camera who want a tactile, offline prompt-and-annotation companion rather than automatic image enhancement.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A photographer wants the physicality and control of a real camera, rejects phone AI enhancements, and asks what people enjoy shooting when the phone stays away.
Tablet users request lower-latency, smoother stylus rendering for fast handwriting, sketching, and ideation, reporting that Goodnotes remains the workaround.

recurrence: Two 2026 requests value deliberate physical capture and responsive handwritten reflection; both reject a generic, friction-heavy digital workflow.
current_workaround: Use a paper notebook, a notes app, Lightroom metadata, or a generic sketch application alongside the camera.
incumbents_and_gap: Lightroom catalogs images and Goodnotes captures handwriting, but neither is a camera-agnostic, prompt-led field notebook that keeps shooting intent, contact-sheet markup, and constraints together offline.
smallest_useful_product: An offline tablet PWA with a short photo-walk prompt deck, a local-import contact sheet, stylus crop/line annotations, and an exportable one-page session sheet. Non-goals: image generation, cloud photo backup, social feed, or RAW development.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, 60% of users complete three walks and mark at least one chosen image with an intentional framing or exposure note before importing it into a full editor.
monetization: one-time — it complements a personal practice and should not turn a private photo archive into a subscription data source.
constraints: Keep images and handwriting on device by default; do not claim calibrated color or RAW support; support stylus, touch, keyboard, and reduced-motion access.
why_distinct: It supports a photographic practice before editing, rather than competing as a camera app, gallery, or AI enhancer.

title: Hex Daily Notebook
user: People who enjoy a short free web puzzle each day and prefer to think with pen-like marks and spatial grids rather than word-game clones.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A daily web-game player asks for more free browser puzzles with a fresh daily challenge and lists several existing word-centric options.
A tldraw user running wargames and TTRPGs requests flat- and pointy-top hex grids because hex maps are a shared spatial reference for many games.

recurrence: Two 2026 requests point to daily browser play and the continuing practical value of hex-grid spatial thinking; the opportunity is a different interaction, not another Wordle skin.
current_workaround: Play word puzzles, print grid puzzles, use a generic whiteboard, or keep scratch paper beside a daily game.
incumbents_and_gap: Puzzmo and many daily sites offer polished word/grid games; virtual tabletops offer hex maps. There is room for a deliberately small, stylus-friendly daily deduction puzzle whose scratch layer is part of play and remains private.
smallest_useful_product: A static PWA serving one deterministic daily hex deduction puzzle, an unlimited local pencil layer with eraser, keyboard alternatives, archive after a delay, and no sign-in. Non-goals: leaderboard, user chat, gambling mechanics, or copied newspaper puzzle formats.
success_measure: At least 30% of first-time players return for three distinct daily puzzles, and median completion or thoughtful abandon happens within 12 minutes.
monetization: free — the utility of a calm daily ritual depends on zero-friction access; a voluntary tip link can cover hosting.
constraints: Generate puzzles from original rules and verify uniqueness; store scratch marks only locally; provide non-color-only clues and keyboard navigation; do not imitate protected puzzle branding.
why_distinct: The core is an original hex spatial-deduction notebook, not a word-game clone or a generic whiteboard.
